Omar Aly Hassan, left, and Ziyad Yaghi were clear on where they stood on terrorism, an acquaintance said. Omar Aly Hassan, Ziyad Yaghi and five others are charged with conspiring to commit violent jihad overseas. An eighth suspect is still being sought, authorities have said. When he lived in Raleigh, Ismail worshipped at the same mosque as Hassan and Yaghi. When groups of young men talked there, Ismail says, the conversation often turned to religion and politics, and Hassan and Yaghi made it clear where they stood. "When it came to something like suicide bombing, they would say, 'If it's a benefit for the Muslims then something like that can be permissible,' " Ismail says. "I could tell it was something they wanted to do." But, he adds, "They never indicated or said 'we are going to make jihad overseas.'" He does not know by whom. He feels they were susceptible to a message of violence "because it sounded cool and exciting." Ismail says he strenuously disagreed with Yaghi and Hassan's views on terrorism even, he says, getting into a public shouting match with them at a restaurant. He says he told them, "You can't do this, man. You can't say it is OK. "That is corruption and terrorism and that is not permissible in Islam." Ismail says he and others raised concerns about Hassan and Yaghi to officials at the Islamic Center of Raleigh, but were "overlooked." "I did my part," Ismail says. Imran Aukhil, a spokesman for the Islamic Center of Raleigh, told CNN on Thursday that he had no information about complaints concerning Hassan and Yaghi. On Saturday, however, he informed CNN that he had researched the matter and learned there was a complaint several years ago against an individual at the mosque. Aukhil said he did not have the name of that person. "It was reported to the FBI," said Aukhil. "The FBI did take note of it in their investigation." WASHINGTON (CNN) -- It's been two years since Humza Ismail began attending graduate school, and in that time he's rarely returned to Raleigh, North Carolina. Still, news that two people he once knew had been taken into custody this week on terrorism-related charges didn't catch him off guard. "To be honest, none of this shocked me," he explains. Both Omar Aly Hassan and Ziyad Yaghi had made their views on terrorism abundantly clear to those around them, according to someone who knew them. Along with five additional individuals, Hassan and Yaghi now face allegations of plotting to engage in violent jihad abroad. Officials have indicated that a search continues for an eighth person connected to the case.

During his time in Raleigh, Ismail attended the same mosque as the two accused men. He recalls that discussions among young men there frequently drifted toward topics of faith and politics, and in these exchanges, Hassan and Yaghi never hid their perspective. "Whenever suicide bombing came up, their position was basically that it could be justified if it served Muslims' interests," Ismail recounts. "It was obvious to me that this was something they aspired to." That said, he clarifies, "I never once heard either of them explicitly announce plans to wage jihad in another country."

According to Ismail, the pair spoke admiringly of Osama bin Laden, describing him using terms like "scholar" and "mujahedeen." "Someone was clearly shaping their thinking," Ismail observes, though he can't identify who that influence might have been. In his view, they were drawn toward violent rhetoric partly because "it had this appeal of being cool and thrilling."

Ismail makes clear he vocally opposed the men's stance on terrorism—so much so that the disagreement once escalated into a heated public argument at a restaurant. He recalls confronting them directly: "This isn't something you can just do. You can't justify it like that. What you're describing is corruption and terrorism, and Islam doesn't allow for that."

According to Ismail, he and several others brought their worries about Hassan and Yaghi to leaders at Raleigh's Islamic Center, but their concerns went unheeded. "I fulfilled my responsibility," he states.

Imran Aukhil, who serves as a spokesperson for the Islamic Center of Raleigh, initially told CNN on Thursday that he wasn't aware of any complaints involving Hassan and Yaghi. By Saturday, though, he had a different answer, telling CNN that after looking into the matter, he discovered a complaint had indeed been filed years earlier against someone associated with the mosque—though he couldn't provide that person's identity. "This was passed along to the FBI," Aukhil confirmed, adding that "the bureau factored it into their investigation."

# Scottish First Minister Humza Yousaf Resigns Amid Political Turmoil

WASHINGTON (CNN) — Humza Yousaf announced his resignation as Scotland's First Minister following weeks of political pressure that threatened to bring down his government through a no-confidence vote.

Yousaf's decision came after his short-lived power-sharing agreement with the Scottish Green Party collapsed, a move that fractured the coalition supporting his leadership of the Scottish National Party (SNP). The end of the coalition left Yousaf's government vulnerable, and opposition parties quickly moved to capitalize on the instability by calling for votes of no confidence.

Facing near-certain defeat in a confidence vote, Yousaf opted to step down rather than continue fighting for a position that had become politically untenable. His resignation marks yet another chapter in the ongoing turbulence that has characterized the SNP's leadership in recent years, following the earlier departure of former First Minister Nicola Sturgeon.

The resignation raises significant questions about the future direction of the SNP and the broader independence movement in Scotland. Yousaf's tenure, though brief, was marked by efforts to navigate the aftermath of Sturgeon's departure while managing internal party tensions and the complexities of coalition governance.

Analysts suggest that the SNP will now face a leadership contest to determine who will steer the party forward, with implications for Scotland's relationship with Westminster and the ongoing debate over independence. The party will need to select a new leader who can unify its factions while addressing the practical challenges of governing without a clear parliamentary majority.

The political upheaval in Edinburgh has drawn attention from international observers, including major news outlets covering the story from Washington and beyond, as it reflects broader patterns of governmental instability seen in various democratic institutions grappling with coalition politics and shifting voter sentiments.

"That's the scary part," the acquaintance added. "It wasn't like there were red flags everyone ignored. It just seemed normal."

CNN has reached out to the FBI's field office and the U.S. Attorney's Office for additional comment on the specifics of the charges and the investigation's origins.

# Eight Charged in Alleged Overseas Jihad Plot; Community Members Say Warning Signs Were Missed

**MINNEAPOLIS** — Federal prosecutors have charged eight men with conspiring to travel abroad to join violent extremist groups, unsealing an indictment Thursday that alleges a coordinated effort spanning more than a year to recruit fighters, raise funds, and arrange passage to conflict zones overseas.

The charges, filed in U.S. District Court, accuse the defendants of violating federal statutes against providing material support to terrorism and conspiring to kill, kidnap, or maim persons in a foreign country. According to the 47-page indictment, the men allegedly used encrypted messaging applications and in-person meetings at private residences to plan their travel and coordinate with contacts affiliated with militant organizations abroad.

"This was not a spontaneous decision by isolated individuals," said the U.S. Attorney for the district, speaking at a news conference. "This was a calculated conspiracy that developed over an extended period, and it involved specific steps — acquiring travel documents, moving money, identifying routes — that reflect premeditation."

Prosecutors say four of the eight defendants had already left the country before their arrest, with two apprehended at international airports attempting to board connecting flights to third countries believed to serve as transit points to conflict regions. The remaining defendants were taken into custody in coordinated early-morning raids.

## Community Says Concerns Fell on Deaf Ears

The arrests have reopened a painful conversation within the local community, where several relatives and community leaders say they had voiced concerns to authorities and to mosque leadership well before any charges were filed.

"I called a hotline eight months ago," said one relative of a defendant, who spoke on condition of anonymity citing fear of retaliation. "I told them my son was talking differently, spending time with people I didn't know, that he'd stopped coming to family gatherings. I was told someone would follow up. No one ever called back."

Community organizers echoed similar frustrations, saying that outreach programs meant to identify and intervene with at-risk individuals were underfunded and inconsistently staffed.

"We have said for years that prevention requires resources and trust-building, not just surveillance," said the director of a local interfaith council that works on countering extremism. "When people do come forward, the system needs to actually respond. Otherwise, why would anyone take that risk again?"

A spokesperson for the FBI's field office said the bureau "takes every tip seriously" and that investigators had in fact opened an inquiry connected to at least one of the defendants earlier in the year, though the spokesperson declined to detail what action, if any, followed that inquiry, citing the ongoing prosecution.

## Mosque Leaders Describe a Difficult Balance

Leaders at the mosque several of the defendants reportedly attended said they had also flagged concerning behavior to congregants' families, but described being caught between wanting to intervene and fear of contributing to broader stigmatization of the community.

"We are constantly walking a line," said the mosque's imam. "If we report every young man who becomes more religious or more withdrawn, we risk treating our own community as suspects. But when something like this happens, people ask why we didn't do more. The truth is we tried, in the ways we could, but we are not law enforcement and we don't have the tools they have."

Civil rights advocates cautioned against drawing broad conclusions from the case, warning that increased scrutiny of Muslim communities in the aftermath of such arrests has historically led to profiling and civil liberties violations.

"Every time one of these cases breaks, the entire community gets treated as a suspect pool," said an attorney with a national Muslim civil rights organization. "The people who tried to raise alarms, who cooperated, who wanted help — they're the ones who often end up facing backlash instead of support."

## What Comes Next

All eight defendants are expected to make initial appearances in federal court this week. If convicted, they face potential sentences of up to 15 years on the material support charges alone, with additional exposure under the conspiracy counts.

The Justice Department said the investigation remains active and that additional charges against other individuals "have not been ruled out."

Family members of several defendants have retained legal counsel and say they intend to cooperate with investigators, while also renewing calls for a broader review of how tips and warning signs are handled by federal and local agencies.

"We're not asking for excuses," the relative who described calling the hotline said. "We're asking why the system that's supposed to catch this didn't catch it, even after we tried to help it."

*This story will be updated as the case develops.*
counterfactuals.label: cf_3
